primary_claim: LLMs' ability to detect that their own conversation history has been tampered with ('prefill awareness') is inconsistent, shallow, and dataset-dependent, but recent Claude models show strong detection when explicitly prompted (Claude Opus 4.6: AUROC 0.80 overall, 0.97 on older-model-style transcripts), while models across the board rarely spontaneously flag tampering when simply asked to continue the conversation.

effect.metric: AUROC for detecting a tampered/injected conversation turn (probability-rating task)
effect.value: Claude Opus 4.6 achieves AUROC 0.80 overall (0.97 on HH-RLHF older-model-style transcripts, 0.39 -- below chance -- on OASST1 human-written transcripts); several older GPT models fall below chance

stated_future_work: Determine whether detection is driven by surface-level style matching or a deeper sense of authorship, potentially using mechanistic interpretability
Clarify the conceptual and empirical relationship between prefill awareness and introspection
Clarify the relationship between prefill awareness, evaluation awareness, and situational awareness more broadly
limitations_stated: The continuation analysis is coarse; it does not measure subtler behavioral shifts like changes in response quality
Internal representations were not measured via probing, so it cannot be ruled out that models 'notice' tampering without verbalizing it
Ideally the prefill would come from the target model actually taking misaligned actions, which is hard to obtain
The elicitation prompt used to measure detection may itself prime models toward suspicion
quote: recent Claude models show rather strong prefill detection capabilities when prompted, suggesting prefill awareness is an emerging and model-specific confound
